extracted.intended_audience: taxpayers, tax preparers, accountants, payroll administrators, and tax compliance professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and eligibility criteria under IRC section 224 and implementing regulations for what counts as a 'qualified tip' and how the deduction is claimed and limited.

rubrics_metrics.name: Qualified tip — voluntary, designated, and in excess of agreed charge
rubrics_metrics.description: A qualified tip is an amount that was voluntarily paid by the payor (customer), designated as a tip by the payor, and is in excess of the amount agreed to be paid for the service.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amounts reclassified by the service provider from the agreed contract price are not qualified tips but are instead part of the charge for services. Example: landscaper charged $4,500 for installation and customer paid additional $600; only $100 is a qualified tip because that amount was determined by and designated by the customer; the additional $500 reclassified from the agreed price is not a tip because it was not paid voluntarily or in excess of the agreed amount.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specified service trade or business exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: An amount received by an individual in the course of a specified service trade or business (as defined in section 199A(d)(2)) is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the individual performs services as an employee, the relevant trade or business is the employer's trade or business; amounts received while performing services for an employer that is a specified service trade or business are not qualified tips regardless of whether the occupation is listed in the tipped-occupation table. See examples in the regulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples applying specified service trade/business rule
rubrics_metrics.description: Illustrative scenarios showing how the specified-service exclusion applies to self-employed and employee situations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example 1: Self-employed comedian's cash tips are not qualified tips because performing arts is a specified service trade or business. Example 2: Hotel-employed pianist's cash tips are qualified because the hotel is not a specified service trade or business and the pianist's occupation is in the Treasury Tipped Occupation Code (TTOC) list. Example 3: Bartender employed by a company that contracts to provide bartending for a theater — tips are qualified when the employer is not engaged in a specified service trade or business and the occupation appears in the TTOC list.

rubrics_metrics.name: Employees using TRDA or GITCA tip-rate reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Employees who enter a Tipped Employee Participation Agreement (TRDA) or a Model Gaming Employee Tip Reporting Agreement (GITCA) may determine qualified tips using the applicable tip rate in their agreement in lieu of reporting actual tips.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of TRDA/GITCA tip rates (and amounts reported on Form 4137 or successor) to determine qualified tips does not affect tip audit protection otherwise applicable to the employee's agreement. Employees remain subject to all other section 224 and regulatory requirements for eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illegal activity exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amount received for a service the performance of which is a felony or misdemeanor under applicable law is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Amounts received for illegal services are categorically excluded from being qualified tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prostitution exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amount received for prostitution services is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prostitution-related receipts are explicitly excluded from qualification as tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pornography exclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Any amount received for pornographic activity is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Receipts for pornographic services or activities are explicitly excluded from qualification as tips.

rubrics_metrics.name: No ownership in or employment by payor
rubrics_metrics.description: A tip received by an employee or other service provider who has an ownership interest in or is employed by the payor of the tip is not a qualified tip.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the tipper is the employer or the payor is an owner/employer of the recipient, the amount does not qualify as a tip for purposes of section 224.

rubrics_metrics.name: Trade-or-business limitation for self-employed taxpayers
rubrics_metrics.description: For qualified tips received by an individual in the course of a trade or business of the individual (other than an employee trade or business), the deduction is allowed only to the extent the trade's gross income (including qualified tips) exceeds the trade's deductible expenses (other than the section 224 tip deduction).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The section 224 deduction is not a trade-or-business deduction for calculating this limit; generally, the deduction under section 224 for self-employed taxpayers is limited to the individual's net income from that trade or business (without regard to the section 224 deduction). Examples: Manicurist with $100,000 gross ($70,000 fees + $30,000 tips) and $40,000 expenses may deduct up to the $25,000 statutory cap; another manicurist with $75,000 gross ($55,000 fees + $20,000 tips) and $60,000 expenses can deduct only $15,000 (the amount by which gross exceeds deductible expenses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social Security number requirement and married-filing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: To claim the section 224 deduction, the taxpayer must include the Social Security number (SSN) of the individual who received the qualified tips on the tax return; married taxpayers must file a joint return to claim the deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only the SSN of the tip-receiving taxpayer is required unless both spouses have qualified tips, in which case SSNs for both are required. The total amount of qualified tips that can be deducted per calendar year is $25,000 regardless of filing status; after applying the $25,000 limitation, the deduction is further subject to the phase-out based on modified adjusted gross income under section 224(b)(2). Example: Married couple J and K with $15,000 and $20,000 in qualified tips respectively may claim a maximum of $25,000 on their joint return for 2025.

rubrics_metrics.name: Occupations eligible — Table 1 (customarily and regularly received tips as of 12/31/2024)
rubrics_metrics.description: Only qualified tips received in connection with occupations listed in Table 1 (occupations that customarily and regularly received tips on or before December 31, 2024) are eligible for the section 224 deduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table 1 provides TTOC codes, occupation titles, descriptions, illustrative examples, and related SOC codes across categories (e.g., Beverage and Food Service, Entertainment and Events, Hospitality, Home Services, Personal Services, Personal Appearance and Wellness, Recreation and Instruction, Transportation and Delivery). An occupation listed in Table 1 is necessary (but not sufficient) for eligibility; the specified service trade or business exclusion still applies (i.e., an occupation in Table 1 does not make tips eligible if earned in a specified service trade or business).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability and termination dates
rubrics_metrics.description: Temporal applicability and termination of the section 224 deduction under these regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This section applies to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024. No deduction shall be allowed under this section for any taxable year beginning after December 31, 2028.
